analysis.one_liner: Raises the estate tax exemption to $1 million and shields family-owned businesses from estate tax.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past a Senate committee referral and received no cosponsors before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised the amount of an estate exempt from the estate tax from $600,000 to $1 million by 2004, fully excluded up to $1 million of qualifying family-owned business or farm assets from the taxable estate, and let heirs pay the tax on the first $1 million above the credit at a 4 percent interest rate over an extended period [S2][S3]. Dorgan, a North Dakota Democrat, framed it as relief for family farms and small businesses whose heirs face tax bills larger than the business's liquid assets [S3]. The exemption increase would apply to every estate, not only family businesses [S3]. The bill went to the Senate Finance Committee, got no cosponsors, and was never acted on before the Congress ended [S4][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of estates large enough to owe estate tax benefit directly: the exemption rises to $1 million for all estates, and owners of family businesses and farms can pass up to $1 million of business assets to heirs tax-free, provided the business makes up half the estate and family members materially participated in running it for at least five of the prior eight years [S3]. The benefit is concentrated among owners of closely held businesses and farms and the heirs of the wealthiest households, since smaller estates already fall under the existing exemption [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Heirs of large estates and family businesses

how_it_helps.text: Phases the estate tax exemption up from $675,000 in 1997 to $1 million by 2004, raising the unified credit against estate and gift tax from the equivalent of a $600,000 exemption [S3].

Excludes up to $1 million of qualifying family-owned business interests from the taxable estate for estates where the business exceeds half the gross estate and family members materially participated for at least five of the previous eight years [S3].

Extends the low 4 percent interest rate on deferred estate tax payments to tax attributable to the first $1 million above the credit amount, reducing the carrying cost for heirs of closely held businesses who spread payments over time [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury bears the lost revenue, which is ultimately a cost borne by taxpayers generally, since the estate tax raises money from a small number of very large estates and the bill shrinks both the tax base and the tax owed on deferred business-estate liabilities [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The exemption increase applies to all estates, not just family businesses, so a large share of the benefit goes to heirs of any decedent leaving more than $675,000, a group concentrated among the wealthiest households [S3].

The family-business exclusion carries a clawback: heirs who stop materially participating in the business or sell it outside the family within 10 years owe additional estate tax with interest, which can trap heirs in a business they might otherwise sell [S3].
Every dollar of foregone estate tax revenue must be made up through other taxes, spending cuts, or borrowing, spreading the cost across taxpayers generally [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The targeted pieces—shielding family businesses whose heirs face tax bills bigger than their liquid assets, and the 4 percent deferral rate—are a genuine, narrowly drawn answer to a real liquidity problem. But the blanket exemption increase to $1 million for all estates delivers most of the tax cut to the heirs of the largest estates without the family-business justification, and the exclusion's 10-year participation rules add complexity and a penalty structure that can bind heirs to a business. On balance the bill's largest benefits flow to concentrated wealth, with the revenue cost spread across everyone else.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, drew no cosponsors, and died there when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Byron Dorgan introduced the Family Estate Tax Relief Act of 1997 on February 6, 1997, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day [S1][S5].
No cosponsors signed on to the bill [S4].
The committee took no further action on the bill, and it received no floor vote before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal treasury kept estate tax revenue that the bill would have foregone, and no estate-tax-paying families or their heirs received the exemption increase or the family-business exclusion from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal treasury kept the revenue

against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no further action—no hearing, markup, or vote

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and died in committee, so no vote ever revealed a partisan split [S4][S5].

industries.note: Owners could pass up to $1 million of business assets to heirs estate-tax-free and defer tax at 4 percent interest, provided family members materially participated in the business. The cost is foregone federal revenue, spread across all taxpayers, though the provision does answer a real liquidity squeeze on heirs of small businesses and farms [S3].
The bill's valuation and ownership rules define qualifying closely held entities whose interests get the exclusion, reducing transfer taxes on ownership stakes in private companies [S3].

The exemption increase to $1 million applies to every estate, not only family businesses, so the largest beneficiaries are heirs of decedents leaving between the old exemption level and $1 million or more [S3].
